questions.stem: For a binary search tree whose keys are distinct, which traversal outputs the keys in ascending order?
explanations: Incorrect — preorder visits root before subtrees and is not generally sorted.
Incorrect — postorder visits children before root and is not generally sorted.
Correct — inorder traversal visits left subtree, node, then right subtree; the BST ordering property makes the output ascending.
Incorrect — level order visits nodes by depth and does not preserve sorted key order.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Programming and Data Structures; source/basis: OpenDSA, Binary Search Trees; inorder traversal.

questions.stem: A recursive factorial routine makes one call for each integer from n down to 1 and uses constant local storage per call. What is its auxiliary call-stack space complexity?
explanations: Incorrect — constant local storage per call does not make the total stack constant when calls accumulate.
Incorrect — the recursion depth decreases by one per call, not by halving n.
Correct — there are Θ(n) simultaneously active calls in the usual recursive implementation, each using O(1) local storage.
Incorrect — no logarithmic factor is introduced by this linear-depth recursion.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Programming and Data Structures; source/basis: Standard data-structures texts; recursion depth and auxiliary stack space.

questions.stem: A topological ordering of all vertices of a directed graph exists if and only if the graph is:
options: A graph in which every vertex has equal in-degree and out-degree
explanations: Incorrect — a complete directed graph with cycles need not have a topological ordering.
Correct — topological ordering is defined for a directed acyclic graph; a directed cycle makes the required ordering impossible.
Incorrect — an undirected tree is not the directed-graph condition for topological ordering.
Incorrect — equal in-degree and out-degree does not imply acyclicity.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; source/basis: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms; topological sorting of DAGs.

questions.stem: For a graph represented by a V×V distance matrix, what is the time complexity of the Floyd–Warshall all-pairs shortest-path algorithm?
explanations: Incorrect — the algorithm examines combinations of source, destination and intermediate vertices.
Incorrect — V² is the matrix size, not the full triple-loop running time.
Correct — three nested loops over vertices give O(V³) time.
Incorrect — there are three, not four, vertex-index loops in the standard algorithm.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; source/basis: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms; all-pairs shortest paths.

questions.stem: A dynamic array doubles its capacity whenever it becomes full. Over a sequence of n append operations, what is the amortized time per append?
explanations: Incorrect — logarithmic resizing events occur, but their total copying cost is linear across n appends.
Correct — geometric growth makes the total number of copied elements O(n), so the amortized append cost is Θ(1).
Incorrect — an individual resize can cost Θ(n), but that is not the amortized cost per append.
Incorrect — the aggregate copying cost does not grow as n log n under doubling.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; source/basis: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms; amortized analysis of dynamic tables.

questions.stem: In the dynamic-programming recurrence for the longest common subsequence of strings X and Y, what is L[i,j] when X[i] equals Y[j]?
explanations: Incorrect — adding the two neighbouring values is not the recurrence for a matching final character.
Correct — when the current characters match, the LCS length is one plus the LCS of the two preceding prefixes.
Incorrect — the maximum-of-neighbours recurrence applies when the characters differ, without the extra 1.
Incorrect — a matching character extends the previous common subsequence rather than resetting it to zero.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; source/basis: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms; dynamic programming and longest common subsequence.

questions.stem: Which language over {a,b} is a standard example of a language recognised by a pushdown automaton but not by a finite automaton?
options: The set of all strings ending in a
The set of strings containing at least one b
explanations: Incorrect — {a,b}* is regular and can be recognised by a finite automaton.
Correct — a PDA can push for each a and pop for each matching b, while a finite automaton cannot remember an unbounded count.
Incorrect — strings ending in a form a regular language.
Incorrect — strings containing at least one b form a regular language.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Theory of Computation; source/basis: Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation; context-free languages and PDAs.

questions.stem: If L is a regular language over alphabet Σ, which language is guaranteed to be regular?
options: Only the finite subsets of L
The set of all non-halting Turing-machine inputs
The set of all context-free languages
explanations: Correct — regular languages are closed under complement; a complete DFA can be complemented by swapping accepting and non-accepting states.
Incorrect — regular languages need not be finite, and this is not a closure operation.
Incorrect — non-halting inputs for arbitrary Turing machines need not form a regular language.
Incorrect — a class of languages is not the complement operation on L.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Theory of Computation; source/basis: Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation; closure properties.

questions.stem: A Turing machine decides a language L if it:
options: Accepts every string and never rejects
May loop forever on strings not in L
Halts on every input, accepting strings in L and rejecting strings not in L
Uses only a finite number of tape cells on every input
explanations: Incorrect — a decider must reject strings outside L as well as accept strings inside L.
Incorrect — looping forever is permitted for a recogniser on some non-members, but not for a decider.
Correct — decidability requires a machine that halts on every input with the correct yes/no answer.
Incorrect — a decider may use unbounded tape as a function of input length; finite-space restriction is not the definition.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Theory of Computation; source/basis: Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation; decidability.

questions.stem: During construction of an LL(1) predictive parsing table, two different productions for the same nonterminal are placed in the same table cell. What does this indicate?
options: The grammar has a parsing-table conflict and is not LL(1) under that table construction
The grammar contains no nullable productions
explanations: Incorrect — an LL(1) table must select at most one production for a nonterminal/lookahead pair.
Correct — a multiple-entry cell creates a predictive parsing conflict, so the grammar is not LL(1) as written.
Incorrect — an LL(1) conflict does not imply the grammar is regular.
Incorrect — conflicts can arise with or without nullable productions.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Compiler Design; source/basis: Aho, Lam, Sethi and Ullman, Compilers; predictive parsing and LL(1) tables.

questions.stem: Why can a directly left-recursive production such as E → E + T cause a naive recursive-descent parser to fail?
options: It makes every token appear as an identifier
It prevents the grammar from generating any finite string
The parser may call the same procedure recursively without consuming input
It forces the parser to use a symbol table before scanning
explanations: Incorrect — left recursion does not change the lexical class of tokens.
Incorrect — left-recursive context-free grammars can generate finite strings.
Correct — a top-down procedure may re-enter E before consuming any input, causing unbounded recursion.
Incorrect — symbol-table construction order is not the cause of this parsing problem.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Compiler Design; source/basis: Aho, Lam, Sethi and Ullman, Compilers; grammar transformations and top-down parsing.

questions.stem: For the expression x = a + b * c, which three-address-code sequence preserves the usual multiplication-before-addition precedence?
options: t1 = a + b; t2 = t1 * c; x = t2
t1 = b * c; t2 = a + t1; x = t2
t1 = a * c; t2 = b + t1; x = t2
x = a + b; t1 = t1 * c
explanations: Incorrect — this sequence adds a and b before multiplying, changing the expression's meaning.
Correct — it computes b*c first, adds a, and assigns the result to x.
Incorrect — it multiplies a and c, which is not the stated expression.
Incorrect — the sequence is incomplete and changes the intended grouping.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Compiler Design; source/basis: Aho, Lam, Sethi and Ullman, Compilers; intermediate-code generation.

questions.stem: A counting semaphore is initialised to 3 and each process must successfully wait on it before entering a protected service. Assuming correct wait/signal use, what is the maximum number of processes simultaneously inside?
explanations: Incorrect — a value of 3 permits more than one concurrent entrant when each entrant consumes one permit.
Incorrect — the semaphore has three permits, not two.
Correct — at most three successful waits can consume the three available permits simultaneously.
Incorrect — the semaphore bounds concurrent entry by its count.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Operating Systems; source/basis: Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts; counting semaphores.

questions.stem: In round-robin CPU scheduling, what tends to happen when the time quantum is made extremely large compared with typical CPU bursts?
explanations: Correct — with a very large quantum, processes usually finish their CPU bursts before pre-emption, so behaviour approaches FCFS.
Incorrect — round-robin does not become SJF merely by increasing its quantum.
Incorrect — a large quantum does not guarantee zero waiting time.
Incorrect — context switches still occur on blocking, completion or other scheduling events.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Operating Systems; source/basis: Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts; CPU scheduling.

questions.stem: In a traditional Unix-like file system, which statement about an inode is correct?
options: It stores the filename as its only content
It stores file metadata and references to data blocks; directory entries map names to inode numbers
It contains the full contents of every file in the directory
It is a network packet used by TCP
explanations: Incorrect — filenames are stored in directory entries, not as the inode's defining content.
Correct — an inode stores metadata and block-location information, while a directory maps a filename to an inode number.
Incorrect — file data resides in data blocks; the inode does not contain every file's complete contents.
Incorrect — an inode is a file-system data structure, not a TCP packet.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Operating Systems; source/basis: Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts; file-system implementation.

questions.stem: In indexed file allocation, where are the addresses of a file's data blocks stored?
options: Only in the first data block
In a separate index block associated with the file
explanations: Incorrect — the first data block contains file data; it is not necessarily the index structure.
Correct — an index block contains pointers to the file's data blocks, allowing non-contiguous allocation and direct block lookup.
Incorrect — the instruction register is part of CPU control, not file-system allocation metadata.
Incorrect — a directory entry does not store the complete block-address list in its name.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Operating Systems; source/basis: Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts; file allocation methods.

questions.stem: Let Enrolled(student, course) contain student-course pairs and Required(course) list all compulsory courses. Which relational-algebra operation returns students enrolled in every course listed in Required?
explanations: Incorrect — union combines tuples from compatible relations; it does not express 'all required courses'.
Incorrect — difference removes tuples and does not test coverage of every required course.
Correct — relational division returns student values paired with all tuples in the divisor relation, matching the 'every required course' condition.
Incorrect — Cartesian product forms all combinations and does not select students who satisfy every required course.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Databases; source/basis: Standard database theory; relational algebra division operator.

questions.stem: Which SQL predicate correctly tests whether column manager_id contains a NULL value?
explanations: Incorrect — comparisons with NULL using = yield UNKNOWN under SQL three-valued logic.
Incorrect — <> NULL also does not test nullness; the result is UNKNOWN.
Correct — IS NULL is the SQL predicate for testing a null value.
Incorrect — NULL is not used as a scalar function in this expression.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Databases; source/basis: PostgreSQL documentation, comparison predicates; standard SQL NULL semantics.

questions.stem: A precedence graph constructed for a schedule of database transactions contains a directed cycle. What follows?
explanations: Incorrect — conflict serializability requires an acyclic precedence graph.
Correct — a directed cycle is the standard test showing that the schedule is not conflict-serializable.
Incorrect — the graph's cycle does not determine whether transactions have committed.
Incorrect — recoverability is a separate property and is not established by the cycle test.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Databases; source/basis: Standard database-system texts; conflict-serializability theorem.

questions.stem: Which B+ tree property makes it particularly useful for range queries?
options: All records are stored only in internal nodes
Leaf nodes are typically linked in key order
Every search must visit every leaf
explanations: Incorrect — B+ trees store data entries or record pointers at the leaves; internal nodes guide search.
Correct — linked leaf nodes allow sequential traversal across an ordered key range after locating the first key.
Incorrect — a range query can scan only the relevant consecutive leaf entries, not every leaf.
Incorrect — B+ trees are height-balanced.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Databases; source/basis: Standard database-system texts; B+ tree indexes and range retrieval.

questions.stem: In a conventional data-flow modelling approach, a context-level DFD represents the system as:
options: A single process interacting with external entities
Every program statement as a separate process
Only the database tables and indexes
explanations: Correct — the context diagram depicts the whole system as one process and shows its data exchanges with external entities.
Incorrect — statement-level decomposition is far below the context level.
Incorrect — a DFD models data flows and processes, not merely the physical database schema.
Incorrect — CPU instruction sequencing is not the purpose of a context DFD.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Information Systems and Software Engineering; source/basis: Sommerville, Software Engineering; data-flow modelling.

questions.stem: Which design combination is generally preferred for a maintainable modular software system?
explanations: Incorrect — unrelated responsibilities and strong interdependence make modules harder to understand and change.
Correct — high cohesion keeps related responsibilities together, while low coupling reduces dependencies between modules.
Incorrect — high cohesion is desirable, but high coupling creates unnecessary inter-module dependence.
Incorrect — the option repeats low cohesion and does not state the preferred design combination.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Information Systems and Software Engineering; source/basis: Sommerville, Software Engineering; modular design quality.

questions.stem: In the software V-model, acceptance testing is most directly associated with validation of which development artefact?
options: The physical database index layout only
explanations: Incorrect — detailed module design is more directly associated with unit-level verification.
Incorrect — formatting rules are not the development artefact validated by acceptance testing.
Correct — acceptance testing checks whether the delivered system satisfies user and business requirements.
Incorrect — database index layout is too narrow to represent the system requirements being accepted.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Information Systems and Software Engineering; source/basis: Standard software-engineering texts; V-model and verification/validation mapping.

questions.stem: A developer changes the authentication module. Which test activity is specifically intended to detect unintended effects on previously working features?
explanations: Correct — regression tests rerun relevant existing tests after a change to detect newly introduced failures.
Incorrect — load testing measures performance under workload and may not reveal functional regressions.
Incorrect — planning acceptance tests does not itself detect side effects of the code change.
Incorrect — code generation is a build activity, not a test activity.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Information Systems and Software Engineering; source/basis: Standard software-engineering texts; regression testing and maintenance.

questions.stem: In cyclic redundancy checking, the sender appends a remainder obtained by:
options: Adding decimal checksums to each byte
Polynomial division over GF(2) using the agreed generator polynomial
Encrypting the frame with the receiver's public key
Counting the number of routers on the path
explanations: Incorrect — CRC is not an ordinary decimal sum of bytes.
Correct — CRC treats bit strings as polynomials over GF(2) and appends the division remainder.
Incorrect — public-key encryption is a different security operation.
Incorrect — router count is unrelated to CRC computation.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Networks; source/basis: Standard data-communications texts; cyclic redundancy check.

questions.stem: OSPF is classified as which type of routing protocol?
options: Distance-vector protocol using hop count only
Link-state protocol that computes shortest paths
Path-vector protocol used only between autonomous systems
explanations: Incorrect — hop-count distance vector describes RIP more closely, not OSPF.
Correct — OSPF distributes link-state information and computes shortest paths using Dijkstra's algorithm.
Incorrect — path-vector routing is associated with BGP.
Incorrect — OSPF is a network-layer routing protocol, not a transport protocol.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Networks; source/basis: IETF RFC 2328, OSPF Version 2 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2328).

questions.stem: In a public-key cryptosystem, A wants to send a confidential message to B. Which key should A use to encrypt the message so that B alone can decrypt it?
explanations: Incorrect — A's private key is not the key used to provide confidentiality to B.
Incorrect — A's public key does not restrict decryption to B.
Incorrect — B's private key must remain secret and is used by B for decryption, not given to A.
Correct — encrypting with B's public key allows the corresponding private key held by B to decrypt the ciphertext.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Networks; source/basis: NIST cryptographic guidance; public-key encryption and key pairs.

questions.stem: When a DNS resolver receives a recursive query from a client, what responsibility does the resolver accept?
options: Return only the address of the root name server
Return the final answer or an error after performing the necessary lookups
Forward the query unchanged to every authoritative server simultaneously
Convert the domain name into an Ethernet MAC address
explanations: Incorrect — returning only a root-server address is a referral, not completion of a recursive query.
Correct — a recursive resolver undertakes the lookup process and returns the requested result or an error to the client.
Incorrect — DNS resolution follows a structured hierarchy; it does not broadcast every query to all authoritative servers.
Incorrect — DNS resolves names to resource records such as IP addresses, not directly to Ethernet MAC addresses.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Networks; source/basis: IETF RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, Domain Names—Concepts and Facilities / Implementation and Specification (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1034; https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035).

questions.stem: Which condition is required for an XML document to be well-formed?
options: It may contain several unrelated root elements
Every element must have the same tag name
It must contain exactly one document element with properly nested start and end tags
Every element must have a DTD declaration
explanations: Incorrect — an XML document has exactly one document element; multiple top-level roots violate well-formedness.
Incorrect — elements may have different names according to the document vocabulary.
Correct — XML well-formedness requires one root document element and properly nested markup.
Incorrect — a DTD is not required merely for an XML document to be well-formed.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Web Technologies; source/basis: W3C XML 1.0 Fifth Edition Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/xml/).

questions.stem: Which statement distinguishes a DOM parser from a SAX parser?
options: DOM builds an in-memory document tree, whereas SAX reports parsing events as the document is read
SAX always builds a complete editable tree before reporting anything
DOM is limited to XML files smaller than one kilobyte
explanations: Correct — DOM exposes a tree representation in memory, while SAX is event-driven and can process a stream incrementally.
Incorrect — SAX is event-driven and does not require building a complete tree.
Incorrect — DOM has no one-kilobyte size restriction; memory use is the practical concern.
Incorrect — low coupling is desirable, but low cohesion means a module groups unrelated responsibilities and is not the preferred design.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Web Technologies; source/basis: W3C XML processing concepts; DOM and SAX parser documentation.

questions.stem: In the standard Java Servlet lifecycle, which sequence is correct for a servlet instance?
options: init(), service() for requests, then destroy()
init() for every request, then compile()
explanations: Incorrect — init() is called before request servicing, not after it.
Incorrect — destruction does not precede initialisation and service.
Correct — the container initialises the servlet, invokes service for requests, and calls destroy before removing the instance.
Incorrect — init() is not called for every request and servlet compilation is not a lifecycle callback.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Web Technologies; source/basis: Jakarta Servlet specification; servlet lifecycle.

questions.stem: In a typical PHP session implementation, what does the browser usually store to let the server associate later requests with session data?
options: A session identifier, commonly carried in a cookie
The PHP source code of the session handler
explanations: Incorrect — session data is normally stored server-side rather than sending the entire session array to the browser.
Correct — the browser typically returns a session identifier, often in a cookie, which lets the server locate session data.
Incorrect — credentials are not stored as the session identifier.
Incorrect — the browser does not receive the server-side PHP handler source code.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Web Technologies; source/basis: PHP manual, Sessions; session identifiers and cookies.

questions.topic: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA
questions.stem: Which C++ feature allows one function algorithm to be written for several compatible data types while retaining compile-time type checking?
explanations: Incorrect — run-time reflection is not the standard mechanism for generic function definitions in C++.
Correct — function templates provide type-parameterised definitions instantiated for compatible argument types.
Incorrect — preprocessor substitution is textual and does not provide template type checking.
Incorrect — multiple inheritance concerns class inheritance, not generic function algorithms.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA; source/basis: ISO C++ standard; function templates and template argument deduction.

questions.topic: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA
questions.stem: A Java reference of type Base refers to an object whose runtime class is Derived. Both classes define an overridden instance method show(). Which implementation is invoked by baseRef.show()?
options: Base.show() always, because the reference type controls overriding
Derived.show(), because overridden instance methods use dynamic dispatch
The compiler reports an error whenever a base reference refers to a derived object
explanations: Incorrect — the declared reference type controls compile-time accessibility, not the target of an overridden instance-method call.
Correct — Java selects the overridden instance method according to the runtime class of the object.
Incorrect — only the selected overriding implementation is invoked through this call.
Incorrect — assigning a derived instance to a compatible base reference is standard polymorphism.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA; source/basis: Java Language Specification, Java SE 21, overriding and dynamic method lookup (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/).

questions.topic: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA
questions.stem: A Java class declares an abstract method export() and also declares a constructor that initialises a name field. Which statement is correct?
options: The constructor makes the class concrete automatically
An abstract class cannot have instance fields
The class may have the constructor and field, but it cannot be instantiated directly while abstract
The abstract method must be static
explanations: Incorrect — declaring a constructor does not implement the abstract method or make the class concrete.
Incorrect — abstract classes may declare and initialise instance fields.
Correct — an abstract class can hold state and define constructors for subclasses, but it cannot itself be instantiated.
Incorrect — abstract instance methods are not declared static.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA; source/basis: Java Language Specification, Java SE 21, abstract classes and constructors (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/).

questions.stem: In a transaction database of 30 baskets, itemset {tea, sugar} appears in 6 baskets. What is its support?
explanations: Incorrect — support is not the raw count expressed as a percentage of 100.
Incorrect — 15% would correspond to 4.5 baskets out of 30.
Correct — support({tea,sugar})=6/30=0.20, or 20%.
Incorrect — 30% would correspond to 9 of the 30 baskets.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; source/basis: Han, Kamber and Pei, Data Mining: Concepts and Techniques; association-rule support.

questions.stem: Among 10 transactions containing item A, 6 also contain item B. What is the confidence of the rule A→B?
explanations: Incorrect — 6 is the co-occurrence count, not 6% confidence.
Incorrect — 40% is the proportion containing A but not B.
Correct — confidence(A→B)=support(A∪B)/support(A)=6/10=60%.
Incorrect — 90% is not supported by the stated counts.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; source/basis: Han, Kamber and Pei, Data Mining: Concepts and Techniques; association-rule confidence.

questions.stem: A rule A→B has confidence 0.60, while item B occurs in 20% of all transactions. What is the lift of the rule?
explanations: Incorrect — 0.12 is the product of confidence and support(B), not the lift.
Incorrect — 0.80 is not the ratio of confidence to support(B).
Incorrect — 1.20 would require a different baseline support or confidence.
Correct — lift=confidence(A→B)/support(B)=0.60/0.20=3.00, indicating positive association relative to independence.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; source/basis: Han, Kamber and Pei, Data Mining: Concepts and Techniques; association-rule lift.

questions.stem: After assigning observations to clusters in K-means, how is each cluster centre updated in the standard algorithm?
options: As the arithmetic mean of the observations assigned to that cluster
As the observation farthest from every other point
As the most frequent categorical label, regardless of feature type
As a random point that is never recalculated
explanations: Correct — the K-means update step sets each centroid to the coordinate-wise mean of its assigned observations.
Incorrect — a farthest point is not the centroid update rule.
Incorrect — a mode may be used in other categorical clustering variants, not standard K-means on numeric vectors.
Incorrect — centroids are recalculated after assignment steps.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; source/basis: scikit-learn User Guide, clustering and K-means (https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html).

questions.stem: For a decision-tree split, information gain is calculated as:
options: Weighted child entropy minus parent entropy
Parent entropy minus the weighted average entropy of the child nodes
The number of leaves multiplied by training accuracy
The Gini impurity of the root divided by the number of features
explanations: Incorrect — this reverses the usual reduction in uncertainty.
Correct — information gain is the parent entropy minus the weighted average entropy after the split.
Incorrect — leaf count and accuracy do not define information gain.
Incorrect — Gini impurity is a separate split criterion, not the stated entropy formula.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; source/basis: Han, Kamber and Pei, Data Mining: Concepts and Techniques; decision-tree induction.

questions.stem: In DBSCAN clustering, a point that is neither a core point nor density-reachable from any core point is classified as:
explanations: Incorrect — DBSCAN does not calculate cluster centroids as part of its basic definition.
Incorrect — support vectors belong to support-vector machines.
Correct — points that cannot be assigned to a density-connected cluster are labelled noise or outliers.
Incorrect — DBSCAN has no requirement for a representative point in every cluster.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; source/basis: Ester et al., A Density-Based Algorithm for Discovering Clusters in Large Spatial Databases; DBSCAN.

questions.stem: The 'naive' assumption in a Naive Bayes classifier is that features are:
options: Mutually exclusive in the training data
Conditionally independent given the class label
explanations: Incorrect — features need not be mutually exclusive.
Correct — Naive Bayes assumes conditional independence of features given the class, simplifying likelihood computation.
Incorrect — Gaussian Naive Bayes uses a normal likelihood for continuous features, but that is not the general defining assumption.
Incorrect — features are used because they provide information about the class label.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; source/basis: Standard machine-learning texts; Naive Bayes conditional-independence assumption.

questions.topic: Current affairs – Regional, National and International
questions.stem: The Union Budget 2026–27 announced India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) 2.0. Which combination most accurately describes its stated focus?
options: Domestic production of semiconductor equipment and materials, development of full-stack Indian semiconductor IP, and stronger supply chains
Universal consumer subsidies for imported smartphones and laptops
A national satellite-navigation replacement for NavIC
A ban on private semiconductor design and fabrication
explanations: Correct — ISM 2.0 targets domestic equipment/material capability, Indian IP and resilient semiconductor supply chains.
Incorrect — Consumer-device subsidies are not the mission's stated design objective.
Incorrect — NavIC is a navigation system, unrelated to semiconductor-manufacturing objectives.
Incorrect — The mission promotes domestic capability; it does not prohibit private design or fabrication.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Current affairs – Regional, National and International; source/basis: Union Budget 2026–27, Notes on Demands for Grants, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, section 14 (https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/eb/allsbe.pdf); Telangana State Portal Cabinet decisions, November 2026 (https://www.telangana.gov.in/news/2026/11/); PRS Telangana Budget Analysis 2026–27 (https://prsindia.org/budgets/states/telangana-budget-analysis-2026-27).

questions.topic: Current affairs – Regional, National and International
questions.stem: A Telangana Cabinet decision reported in November 2026 approved replacing the combined Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Commission with separate commissions. What composition was specified for each proposed commission?
explanations: Incorrect — The announced composition is larger than three members.
Correct — The Cabinet release specifies one Chairperson and five members for each separate commission.
Incorrect — The release specifies a single Chairperson, not five.
Incorrect — The specified membership is five members in addition to the Chairperson.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Current affairs – Regional, National and International; source/basis: Union Budget 2026–27, Notes on Demands for Grants, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, section 14 (https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/eb/allsbe.pdf); Telangana State Portal Cabinet decisions, November 2026 (https://www.telangana.gov.in/news/2026/11/); PRS Telangana Budget Analysis 2026–27 (https://prsindia.org/budgets/states/telangana-budget-analysis-2026-27).

questions.topic: Current affairs – Regional, National and International
questions.stem: According to PRS Legislative Research's analysis of the Telangana Budget 2026–27, the State targeted a fiscal deficit of approximately what percentage of GSDP?
explanations: Incorrect — This is materially below the budget target reported by PRS.
Incorrect — The reported target is higher than 2.0%.

questions.stem: Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which statement best describes a coastal State's exclusive economic zone (EEZ)?
options: It extends up to 200 nautical miles from the baselines, where the coastal State has specified sovereign rights over natural resources but not full territorial sovereignty
It extends exactly 200 kilometres from the coastline and gives the coastal State complete sovereignty over all navigation
It is a zone in which only the flag State of a passing vessel may exploit natural resources
It begins only beyond the continental shelf and has no fixed maximum distance
explanations: Correct — UNCLOS Part V sets an outer limit of 200 nautical miles from baselines and grants resource-related rights, not full sovereignty.
Incorrect — The distance is measured in nautical miles from baselines; an EEZ is not territorial sea.
Incorrect — Resource rights belong to the coastal State, subject to UNCLOS, not to passing vessels.
Incorrect — Article 57 specifies a maximum breadth; it is not limited to waters beyond the continental shelf.

questions.stem: A WTO member reduces the customs duty on a particular imported product from one WTO member. Subject to recognised exceptions, what does the GATT most-favoured-nation principle generally require?
options: The reduced treatment must be extended immediately and unconditionally to like products from all WTO members
The reduced treatment may be reserved permanently for the first trading partner
The reduction must apply only to products from neighbouring countries
The importing member must impose the same tariff on every product category
explanations: Correct — GATT Article I:1 generally extends an advantage to like products of all members immediately and unconditionally.
Incorrect — MFN is non-discriminatory; it does not permit a permanent preference except under recognised exceptions.
Incorrect — Geographical proximity is not the general test under Article I:1.
Incorrect — MFN concerns like products across members, not identical tariffs for unrelated product categories.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: International Relations and Events; source/basis: UNCLOS 1982, Part V, Articles 56–57; GATT 1994, Article I:1; WTO principles.

A change in the chemical composition of the atmosphere above the detector
A shift in the Earth's magnetic pole measured by a compass
A change in the speed of sound through a vacuum chamber

Incorrect — Atmospheric chemistry is not the measured signal in a laser interferometer.

questions.stem: In the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing system, what is the primary role of the guide RNA?
options: It directs the Cas9 nuclease to a complementary target DNA sequence adjacent to a suitable PAM
It repairs every DNA break by independently synthesising a complete chromosome
It converts DNA directly into a protein without transcription
It prevents Cas9 from binding to any DNA sequence
explanations: Correct — The guide RNA base-pairs with the target and positions Cas9 near a compatible PAM for cleavage.
Incorrect — Cellular repair pathways repair DNA; guide RNA does not synthesise a chromosome.

The water contains no dissolved organic matter
The river's salinity has necessarily increased
Photosynthesis has stopped permanently throughout the river basin

Its total population increases regardless of age composition or labour-market conditions
The proportion of elderly people becomes larger than the working-age population

questions.stem: A control system follows two rules: if pump P runs, valve V must be open; if valve V is open, sensor S is active. During a test, sensor S is not active. Which conclusion follows from the rules?
options: Valve V is not open and pump P is not running
Valve V is open but pump P is stopped
No conclusion about either valve V or pump P is possible
explanations: Incorrect — If P ran, V would be open and S would be active, contradicting the observation.
Correct — By modus tollens, S inactive implies V closed; then P cannot be running because P requires V open.
Incorrect — This contradicts the rule that an open V makes S active.
Incorrect — The rules permit both conclusions by applying modus tollens twice.

Allow the read and reset the write-timestamp of X to TS(Tᵢ)
Wait until every other transaction commits, then perform the read

options: Both 0 and 1 simultaneously as two classical output bits
A definite outcome, 0 or 1, with probabilities |α|² and |β|² respectively
An outcome determined only by the larger of α and β, regardless of magnitude
explanations: A measurement does not return two classical bits from one qubit.
Correct. The Born rule gives outcome probabilities |α|² for 0 and |β|² for 1.
The probabilities depend on squared amplitudes, not merely which amplitude is larger.
A single qubit measured in this basis has two possible outcomes, not 256.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: General Science; India’s Achievements in Science and Technology; source/basis: NIST, Introduction to Quantum Information Science; qubits and measurement.

questions.topic: Environmental issues; Disaster Management – Prevention and Mitigation Strategies
questions.stem: A persistent, fat-soluble pollutant is measured at increasing concentrations in plankton, small fish and predatory fish. Which process best explains the rise at successive trophic levels?
explanations: Biodegradation breaks down substances and does not explain increasing concentration up the food chain.
Correct. Biomagnification is the increase in concentration of a persistent contaminant at higher trophic levels.
Nitrogen fixation converts atmospheric nitrogen into biologically usable forms.
Primary succession describes ecological development on a newly exposed substrate.

questions.topic: Environmental issues; Disaster Management – Prevention and Mitigation Strategies
questions.stem: Why can an intact wetland reduce the peak discharge of a nearby river during a heavy rainfall event?
options: It permanently prevents all rainfall from reaching the river
It stores and slowly releases water, increasing temporary storage and attenuating flow
It converts surface water directly into oxygen
It increases the velocity of every tributary
explanations: Wetlands cannot stop all rainfall or eliminate every flood.
Correct. Wetland storage and slower release can delay runoff and reduce peak flows, although protection is not absolute.
Oxygen production is not the hydrological mechanism responsible for flood attenuation.
Increasing tributary velocity would generally not explain a reduction in peak discharge.

questions.topic: Environmental issues; Disaster Management – Prevention and Mitigation Strategies
questions.stem: A rapidly urbanising catchment replaces vegetated soil with roofs, concrete and asphalt. If drainage capacity is unchanged, what is the most direct hydrological effect?
options: Infiltration rises and surface runoff falls
Infiltration falls and faster surface runoff can raise the flood peak
Evapotranspiration becomes the only source of streamflow
explanations: Impervious cover generally reduces, rather than increases, infiltration.
Correct. Less infiltration and quicker runoff can increase runoff volume and peak flow.
Groundwater recharge usually does not double when permeable surfaces are replaced.
Streams continue to receive rainfall runoff and other flows; evapotranspiration is not their only source.

questions.topic: Economic and Social Development of India and Telangana

options: It indicates measured income inequality between the two theoretical extremes of 0 and 1
It means exactly 32% of the population is below the poverty line
explanations: A Gini value of 0, not 0.32, represents perfect equality on this scale.
A value of 1 represents maximal inequality in the standard interpretation.
Correct. A Gini of 0.32 is an inequality measure between the equality and maximal-inequality endpoints.
The Gini coefficient is not a headcount poverty ratio and does not directly give the share below a poverty line.

82% would use a numerator or denominator not supplied in the question.
52% has no basis in the stated labour-force counts.

questions.stem: A factory's emissions impose health costs on nearby residents that the factory does not pay. In the standard externality model, which policy most directly seeks to internalise this cost?
options: A Pigouvian tax linked to marginal external damage
A subsidy for every additional unit of pollution
A price ceiling on the factory's output
A reduction in the legal liability of the polluter
explanations: Correct. A Pigouvian tax can make the producer face the external cost, moving private incentives toward social cost.
A pollution subsidy increases the incentive to emit rather than internalising the damage.
An output price ceiling does not directly price the marginal pollution damage.
Reducing liability weakens rather than internalises the external cost.

questions.topic: Physical, Social and Economic Geography of India
questions.stem: Moisture-laden south-west monsoon winds encounter the Western Ghats. Which pattern is most consistent with orographic rainfall?
options: The leeward Deccan side is generally wetter than the windward Konkan side
The windward western slopes receive heavy rain while areas east of the crest lie in a relative rain shadow
Both sides receive identical rainfall because elevation has no effect
Rainfall occurs only on the highest peaks and nowhere else
explanations: The western windward slopes generally receive more, not less, orographic rainfall.
Correct. Forced ascent cools moist air and produces heavy windward rainfall; descending air is relatively drier east of the crest.
Elevation and forced ascent strongly affect rainfall distribution.
Rainfall is not restricted to the highest peaks; broad windward slopes receive substantial rain.

questions.topic: Physical, Social and Economic Geography of India
questions.stem: Which statement best describes the Narmada River's major geographical setting?
options: It flows east through the Ganga alluvial plain
It flows west through a rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges
It is a Himalayan river fed mainly by glaciers
It drains into the Bay of Bengal through the Mahanadi delta
explanations: The Narmada is a west-flowing peninsular river, not an east-flowing Ganga tributary.
Correct. It follows a rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges and reaches the Arabian Sea.
Its source and regime are peninsular, not Himalayan-glacial.
The Narmada drains west to the Arabian Sea, not into the Mahanadi delta.

Khadar is newer alluvium renewed by floods; Bangar is older alluvium generally on higher terraces
Both terms refer only to black cotton soil
Bangar is coastal laterite while Khadar is desert sand
explanations: This reverses the conventional age and position distinction.
Correct. Khadar is newer floodplain alluvium, whereas Bangar is older alluvium, commonly on slightly higher ground.
Neither term denotes black cotton soil.
The terms classify alluvial deposits, not laterite and desert sand.

Reserved seats for the Depressed Classes were provided within joint electorates

Separate electorates were created for every religious community

questions.stem: Which proposal was central to the Wavell Plan discussed at the 1945 Simla Conference?
options: An Executive Council composed of Indian members except the Viceroy and Commander-in-Chief, with parity between caste Hindus and Muslims
Immediate transfer of sovereignty to provincial governments without a Constituent Assembly
A separate sovereign state for every province
A directly elected Indian President replacing the Viceroy
explanations: Correct. The plan proposed a reconstituted Executive Council with Indian members other than the Viceroy and Commander-in-Chief, and parity between caste Hindus and Muslims.
The Wavell Plan did not immediately transfer sovereignty to provinces.

Expansion of the Viceroy's Executive Council and a post-war constitution-making process, subject to minority safeguards
Acceptance of the Cabinet Mission's three-tier federation
Abolition of the office of Viceroy

The three-tier grouping plan belonged to the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946.
The Viceroy's office was not abolished by the August Offer.

questions.stem: A component lifetime T is exponentially distributed with rate λ = 0.2 per hour. Given that it has already survived 4 hours, what is P(T > 10 | T > 4)?
explanations: e^(−2) is the unconditional probability P(T>10), not the conditional probability.
Correct. By memorylessness, P(T>10|T>4)=P(T>6)=e^(−0.2×6)=e^(−1.2).
e^(−0.8) uses only the already-survived four hours.
1−e^(−1.2) is the probability of failure within the next six hours, not survival beyond it.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Probability and Statistics; source/basis: OpenStax, Introductory Statistics 2e; ILO statistical definitions.

questions.subtopic: Central limit theorem for a sample mean
questions.stem: A population has mean 50 and standard deviation 12. For a sufficiently large random sample of size 36, what are the approximate mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean?
explanations: The sample-mean standard deviation is smaller than the population standard deviation.
Correct. E(X̄)=50 and SE(X̄)=σ/√n=12/6=2.
The mean of the sampling distribution remains the population mean, not the sample size.
6 would result from dividing by √4 rather than √36.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Probability and Statistics; source/basis: OpenStax, Introductory Statistics 2e; ILO statistical definitions.

questions.subtopic: Marginal density from a joint probability density
questions.stem: A joint density is f(x,y)=2 on the triangular region 0 < x < y < 1 and zero elsewhere. What is the marginal density fX(x) for 0 < x < 1?
explanations: Integrating the constant density from y=x to 1 gives 2(1−x), not 2x.
Correct. fX(x)=∫ from x to 1 of 2 dy = 2(1−x).
1−x² is not the integral of the given joint density over the permitted y-range.
The marginal is obtained by integration, not division by the remaining interval length.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Probability and Statistics; source/basis: OpenStax, Introductory Statistics 2e; ILO statistical definitions.

questions.subtopic: Order of an element in a finite additive group
questions.stem: In the additive group Z₁₂, what is the order of the element 8?
explanations: 2×8 = 16 ≡ 4 (mod 12), not the identity 0.
Correct. 8, 8+8 ≡ 4, and 8+8+8 ≡ 0 (mod 12), so the order is 3.
Four additions are not the first time the identity is reached.
Six additions are also a multiple of the order, but not the least positive one.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Set Theory & Algebra; Linear Algebra; source/basis: David C. Lay et al., Linear Algebra and Its Applications, 6th ed.

questions.stem: What is the multiplicative inverse of 7 modulo 26?
explanations: Correct. 7×15 = 105 = 4×26 + 1, so 15 is the inverse modulo 26.

questions.subtopic: Consistency of a linear system by ranks
questions.stem: A system Ax=b has 4 unknowns. If rank(A)=rank([A|b])=2, how many free variables does its solution set have?
explanations: Zero free variables would require rank 4 for a unique solution.
One free variable would require rank 3.
Correct. The system is consistent and has 4−2=2 free variables.
Four free variables would require rank zero.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Set Theory & Algebra; Linear Algebra; source/basis: David C. Lay et al., Linear Algebra and Its Applications, 6th ed.

questions.stem: In R⁴, let v₁=(1,0,1,0), v₂=(0,1,1,0), v₃=(1,1,2,0) and v₄=(0,0,0,1). What is dim(span{v₁,v₂,v₃,v₄})?
explanations: The span is not one-dimensional because v₁ and v₂ are independent.
It is not two-dimensional because v₄ adds an independent fourth-coordinate direction to v₁ and v₂.
Correct. v₃=v₁+v₂, while v₁, v₂ and v₄ are independent; the dimension is 3.
The four listed vectors are not all independent because v₃=v₁+v₂.

questions.topic: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Graph Theory; Mathematical Logic
questions.stem: How many onto functions are there from a set containing 4 elements to a set containing 2 elements?
explanations: 8 counts only a subset of all functions and has no surjectivity adjustment.
12 is not obtained by excluding the two constant functions from 16.
Correct. There are 2⁴ total functions; subtract the two constant non-onto functions to get 14.
16 counts all functions, including the two that miss one codomain element.

questions.subtopic: Chromatic number of an odd cycle
questions.stem: What is the chromatic number of the cycle graph C₇?
explanations: A cycle with edges cannot be coloured with one colour.
An odd cycle is not bipartite, so two colours are insufficient.
Correct. Every odd cycle requires three colours, and three suffice.
Seven colours are unnecessary; three are sufficient.

questions.subtopic: Perfect matchings in a complete bipartite graph
questions.stem: How many distinct perfect matchings does the complete bipartite graph K₃,₃ contain?
explanations: There are more than three one-to-one pairings of the two three-vertex parts.
Correct. Each perfect matching corresponds to a bijection between the two parts, giving 3! = 6.
Nine is the total number of edges, not the number of perfect matchings.
Twelve is not the count of bijections between two three-element sets.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Graph Theory; Mathematical Logic; source/basis: Kenneth Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, 8th ed.

questions.subtopic: Maximum edges in a complete bipartite graph
questions.stem: A complete bipartite graph has part sizes 4 and 6. How many edges does it contain?
explanations: 10 is the sum of the part sizes, not the edge count.
20 omits four possible cross-part edges.
Correct. Every vertex in the first part connects to all six in the second, so |E|=4×6=24.
36 would require part sizes whose product is 36.

questions.stem: A 3-to-8 active-high decoder has its enable asserted and inputs A₂A₁A₀=101. Which output is asserted?
explanations: Y₁ corresponds to input 001, not 101.
Y₃ corresponds to input 011.
Correct. Binary 101 represents decimal 5, so output Y₅ is asserted.
Y₇ corresponds to input 111.

questions.stem: A standard n-stage Johnson counter feeds the complemented output of the last flip-flop back to the first stage. How many distinct states does an ideal n-stage Johnson counter cycle through?
explanations: n is the number of stages, not the standard state count.
Correct. A Johnson counter with n stages has 2n distinct states in its normal cycle.
2^n is the state count of an unrestricted n-bit register, not this Johnson sequence.
2^n - 1 is not the Johnson-counter state-count formula.

questions.stem: In IEEE 754 binary32 (single precision), how many bits are assigned to the exponent field and what is its bias?
explanations: Binary32 uses an 8-bit exponent, not 7 bits.
Correct. Binary32 has 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits with bias 127, and 23 fraction bits.
Eleven exponent bits and bias 1023 are used in binary64, not binary32.
Twenty-three bits are the fraction field, not the exponent field.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Digital Logic; source/basis: M. Morris Mano and Michael Ciletti, Digital Design, 6th ed.; IEEE 754-2019.

questions.stem: In a conventional programmable logic array (PLA), which parts of the logic structure are programmable?
options: Both the AND plane and the OR plane
explanations: Input buffers alone do not define the PLA's programmable product-term and sum structure.
Correct. A PLA has programmable AND and OR arrays, allowing product terms to be combined into outputs.
Output pins are not the two logic planes being programmed.
A PLA is distinguished by programmability of both planes.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Digital Logic; source/basis: M. Morris Mano and Michael Ciletti, Digital Design, 6th ed.; IEEE 754-2019.

questions.stem: In a conventional load–store RISC architecture, which statement is generally correct?
options: Arithmetic instructions may directly use arbitrary memory operands
Only load and store instructions access data memory; arithmetic operations use registers
Every instruction must access the cache twice
The program counter is stored only in main memory
explanations: A pure load–store design restricts arithmetic operands to registers rather than arbitrary memory locations.
Correct. Data memory is accessed by explicit load/store instructions; arithmetic and logical operations work on registers.
There is no rule requiring two cache accesses for every instruction.
The program counter is a processor register, not a value stored only in main memory.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Organization and Architecture; source/basis: Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design, RISC-V Edition, 2nd ed.

questions.stem: In a microprogrammed control unit, the control signals for a machine instruction are generated primarily from:
options: Microinstructions stored in a control memory and sequenced by a microsequencer
A fixed combinational truth table with no stored control words
The contents of the instruction cache alone
explanations: Correct. A microprogrammed controller fetches control words from control memory and sequences them to generate control signals.
This describes a hardwired-control approach rather than microprogrammed control.
An instruction cache stores instructions, not the microprogram's control words.
The process table is an OS data structure and does not generate CPU micro-operations.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Organization and Architecture; source/basis: Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design, RISC-V Edition, 2nd ed.

questions.stem: A RAID 5 array distributes data and parity blocks across its member disks. What is its usual single-disk-failure tolerance?
options: No disk may fail without total data loss
It can tolerate one failed disk and reconstruct its contents from the remaining data and parity
It can tolerate any two failed disks
It stores three complete mirrored copies of every block
explanations: RAID 5 is designed to survive one disk failure, not zero.
Correct. Distributed parity allows reconstruction after one member disk fails.
Two simultaneous disk failures generally exceed RAID 5's parity protection.
Three-way mirroring describes a different redundancy strategy, not RAID 5.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Organization and Architecture; source/basis: Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design, RISC-V Edition, 2nd ed.

questions.stem: A program has 80% of its execution time parallelisable and 20% inherently serial. According to Amdahl's law, what is the maximum speedup as the number of processors tends to infinity?
explanations: 2 is below the limiting speedup.
4 is below the theoretical limit for this serial fraction.
Correct. The limit is 1/serial fraction = 1/0.20 = 5.
10 would require a serial fraction of 10%.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Organization and Architecture; source/basis: Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design, RISC-V Edition, 2nd ed.

questions.stem: An empty AVL tree receives keys 30, 20 and 10 in that order. Which rotation restores balance after the third insertion?
explanations: A left rotation would move the heavy left subtree in the wrong direction.
Correct. The sequence creates a left-left imbalance at 30, repaired by a single right rotation.
A left-right rotation is used for a left-right, not left-left, imbalance.
A right-left rotation is used for a right-left imbalance.

questions.stem: What is the worst-case time complexity of building a binary heap from an arbitrary array using the standard bottom-up heapify procedure?
explanations: The procedure must process many nodes, so it is not logarithmic overall.
Correct. Summing the bounded sift-down work by node height gives linear total time.
Repeated insertion takes Θ(n log n), but bottom-up heap construction is asymptotically faster.
Quadratic time is not required by bottom-up heapify.

questions.stem: Assume a C implementation gives int alignment and size of 4 bytes, char size and alignment of 1 byte, and no packing extensions. What is sizeof(struct S) for `struct S { char c; int i; char d; };`?
explanations: Six ignores required padding before the int and at the end of the structure.
Eight accounts for initial padding but not the final alignment padding.
Correct. Layout is char at 0, padding to 4, int at 4–7, char at 8, then padding to a 4-byte multiple: 12 bytes.
Sixteen adds padding not required by the stated alignments.

questions.subtopic: Safe use of realloc in C
questions.stem: A program must resize a heap block with realloc while preserving access to the original block if allocation fails. Which idiom is safest?
options: Assign realloc directly to the only pointer variable
Store realloc's result in a temporary pointer and update the original pointer only if the result is non-NULL
Free the original block before calling realloc
Call realloc with a NULL size and assume the block is unchanged
explanations: Direct assignment can lose the only pointer to the original block if realloc returns NULL.
Correct. A temporary preserves the original pointer on failure; assign it back only after success.
Freeing first destroys the data that realloc is meant to preserve.
A zero-size request has implementation-specific deallocation implications and is not a safe resize idiom.

questions.stem: For the standard 0/1 knapsack dynamic-programming algorithm with n items and integer capacity W, what is its usual time complexity?
explanations: The standard table considers item-capacity pairs, not a logarithmic number of capacities.
Correct. Each of n items updates up to W capacity states, giving Θ(nW) time.
W² omits the dependence on the number of items and is not the standard bound.
Exhaustive subset enumeration is exponential; dynamic programming is pseudo-polynomial.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; source/basis: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms, 4th ed.

questions.stem: For sorting n distinct keys using only comparisons, what is the asymptotic worst-case lower bound on the number of comparisons?
explanations: A linear lower bound is too weak; the comparison decision tree must distinguish n! orders.
A logarithmic lower bound is far below the decision-tree requirement.
Correct. A comparison decision tree needs at least n! leaves, giving Ω(log(n!)) = Ω(n log n).
The lower bound is not quadratic-logarithmic; optimal comparison sorts achieve Θ(n log n).
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; source/basis: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms, 4th ed.

questions.stem: For distinct input keys and independently randomised pivots, what is the expected running time of randomized quicksort?
explanations: A comparison sort must inspect enough keys to order them; linear time is not the expected bound.
Correct. Random pivot choices give expected Θ(n log n), although a worst-case sequence can still take Θ(n²).
Quadratic time is the worst case, not the expected time under random pivots.
Logarithmic time is insufficient even to inspect all n keys.

questions.subtopic: Definition of an NP-complete decision problem
questions.stem: A decision problem C is NP-complete when which pair of conditions holds?
options: C is in P and every problem in P reduces to C
C is in NP and every problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to C
C is undecidable and every undecidable problem reduces to C
C is solvable only by a nondeterministic machine in constant time
explanations: Membership in P alone does not establish NP-completeness.
Correct. NP-completeness requires membership in NP and NP-hardness via polynomial-time reductions from all NP problems.
NP-complete problems are decidable; undecidability is not part of the definition.
Nondeterministic polynomial-time solvability is the relevant class condition, not constant time.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; source/basis: Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms, 4th ed.

questions.stem: Which language over {a,b,c} is a standard example of a language that is not context-free?
options: {w | w contains an even number of a symbols}
explanations: A single-stack pushdown automaton can recognise equal counts of a's followed by b's.
Correct. Matching three ordered blocks of equal size exceeds the power of a context-free grammar; the CFL pumping lemma proves non-context-freeness.
The concatenation a* b* is regular, hence context-free.
Parity of a symbols is regular, hence context-free.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Theory of Computation; source/basis: Michael Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares deterministic context-free languages (DCFLs) with context-free languages (CFLs)?
options: DCFLs form a proper subset of CFLs
CFLs are a proper subset of regular languages
A deterministic PDA has two independent stacks
explanations: Nondeterminism is required for some context-free languages; not every CFL is deterministic.
Correct. Every DCFL is context-free, but some CFLs cannot be recognised by a deterministic PDA.
Regular languages are a subset of CFLs, not a superset of all CFLs.
A standard PDA has one stack; two stacks would greatly increase computational power.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Theory of Computation; source/basis: Michael Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

questions.stem: A Turing machine accepts every string in language L, rejects some strings not in L, but may loop forever on other strings not in L. How is L classified by this machine?
options: Recursively enumerable (recognisable), but not necessarily decidable
explanations: A decider must halt on every input, which is not guaranteed here.
Correct. A recogniser may loop on non-members; this guarantees recognisability but not decidability.
The description gives no reason for L to be finite.
Turing recognisability alone does not imply regularity.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Theory of Computation; source/basis: Michael Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

questions.subtopic: Computational power of a two-stack PDA
questions.stem: What is the standard computational-power result for a pushdown automaton equipped with two independent stacks?
options: It is equivalent in computational power to a Turing machine
It is weaker than a one-stack PDA
It can recognise only finite languages
explanations: Two stacks can store and manipulate substantially more than finite-state memory.
Correct. Two stacks can simulate the left and right portions of a Turing-machine tape, giving Turing-equivalent power.
Adding a second stack increases, rather than reduces, computational power.
The machine is not restricted to finite languages.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Theory of Computation; source/basis: Michael Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

questions.stem: Consider the numbered intermediate-code instructions: 1: a=b+c; 2: if a>0 goto 5; 3: d=e*f; 4: goto 6; 5: d=e*f; 6: return d. Which set contains all basic-block leaders?
explanations: Instruction 2 is a conditional jump, but it is not a leader merely because it is a jump; instruction 3 follows it.
Correct. Instruction 1 starts the code; 3 follows a conditional jump; 5 and 6 are jump targets, and 6 also follows a jump.
The set omits the first instruction and the target 6.
The set misses the instruction following the conditional jump and the target 5.

questions.stem: A compiler moves an expression from inside a loop to immediately before the loop. Under what condition is this loop-invariant code motion generally valid?
options: The expression's operands are unchanged by every loop iteration and moving it preserves observable behaviour
The expression must contain a volatile read on every iteration
The expression must modify the loop counter
The expression must throw an exception on every iteration
explanations: Correct. If operands do not change and execution/exception semantics are preserved, the expression need not be recomputed each iteration.
Volatile reads are observable and generally cannot be freely hoisted.
Changing the loop counter would alter control flow rather than identify an invariant expression.
An expression that throws each iteration cannot generally be moved outside without changing behaviour.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Compiler Design; source/basis: Aho, Lam, Sethi and Ullman, Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools, 2nd ed.

questions.stem: At a program point, a variable is considered live when:
options: Its current value may be used along some path before the variable is redefined
It has already been written to disk
It is declared globally, regardless of future use
Its storage address is known at compile time
explanations: Correct. Liveness means the current value can be read before being overwritten on a reachable path.
Disk persistence is unrelated to compiler liveness.
A global variable can be dead if its current value is never used.
Knowing an address does not establish that the stored value will be used.

questions.stem: Which compiler transformation replaces a compile-time constant expression such as `6 * 7` with its value `42`?
explanations: Loop unrolling duplicates loop-body instructions to reduce loop overhead.
Correct. Constant folding evaluates expressions whose operands are known constants during compilation.
Register spilling moves values between registers and memory when register pressure is high.
Common-subexpression elimination reuses an already-computed expression rather than simply evaluating constants.

questions.stem: In a priority-based CPU scheduler, what is the purpose of aging?
options: To lower the priority of processes that have waited longest
To gradually raise the priority of waiting processes so that starvation is reduced
To increase the time quantum after every context switch
To terminate processes that miss a deadline
explanations: Lowering the priority of long-waiting processes would worsen starvation.
Correct. Aging increases a waiting process's priority over time, improving its chance of service.
Time-quantum adjustment is not the defining purpose of priority aging.
Aging is a scheduling fairness mechanism, not a termination rule.

questions.stem: What is the principal purpose of journaling in a file system?
options: To record intended metadata or file-system updates so recovery can restore consistency after a crash
To encrypt every user file with a different public key
To eliminate the need for disk blocks
To guarantee that no hardware failure can lose user data
explanations: Correct. A journal records operations or metadata updates so the file system can recover a consistent state after interruption.
Encryption is a separate security function.
Journaling still uses disk blocks to store file-system data and metadata.
Journaling improves consistency but cannot guarantee against every hardware failure or all data loss.

questions.stem: Two processes communicate through a shared-memory region mapped into both address spaces. What additional mechanism is normally needed when they update shared data concurrently?
options: Explicit synchronisation such as a mutex or semaphore
A separate TCP connection for every variable
explanations: DNS resolves names and does not coordinate concurrent memory updates.
Correct. Shared memory provides a common data region, while locks or other synchronisation prevent races.
A TCP connection is not required for processes sharing mapped memory on the same system.
Compiler flags do not provide inter-process mutual exclusion.

questions.stem: In the Clock (second-chance) page-replacement algorithm, what does the algorithm do when the page at the current hand position has its reference bit set to 1?
options: Replace it immediately without changing the bit
Clear the reference bit and advance the hand, giving the page a second chance
Pin the page permanently in physical memory
Swap the page to disk and halt the process
explanations: A set reference bit indicates recent use, so immediate replacement is not the second-chance rule.
Correct. The algorithm clears the bit and advances the hand; a later pass may replace the page if it remains unreferenced.
The algorithm does not permanently pin pages.
A page replacement does not normally halt the process.

questions.subtopic: Fourth normal form and multivalued dependencies

The relation has no foreign keys

The dependent attribute set need not itself be a candidate key.
Foreign keys are not prohibited by 4NF.
Atomic attributes are a 1NF requirement and do not alone establish 4NF.

questions.stem: A SQL query uses `A LEFT OUTER JOIN B ON A.id = B.id`. What happens to a row of A that has no matching row in B?

The row from A is retained and columns from B are filled with NULL
The row from A is duplicated once for every row in B
The query automatically converts to an INNER JOIN

Unmatched rows are not duplicated for each unrelated row in B.
A LEFT OUTER JOIN does not become an INNER JOIN automatically.

Every transaction commits at exactly the same time
No transaction ever reads data written by another transaction
All writes occur before all reads
explanations: Correct. Preventing reads of uncommitted writes avoids cascading aborts.
Simultaneous commit times are not required.
Transactions may read other transactions' committed values.
A cascadeless schedule need not place every write before every read.

questions.subtopic: UML use-case include and extend relationships
questions.stem: In a UML use-case diagram, what is the usual distinction between `<<include>>` and `<<extend>>`?
options: Include represents required reused behaviour; extend adds conditional or optional behaviour at an extension point

questions.stem: A storage tank is 60% full. After 120 litres are added, it becomes 80% full. What is the tank's total capacity?
explanations: A 400-litre tank would gain only 80 litres between 60% and 80%.
A 500-litre tank would gain 100 litres over that interval.
Correct. The 20-percentage-point increase equals 120 litres, so capacity = 120/0.20 = 600 litres.
An 800-litre tank would require 160 litres for a 20-point increase.

questions.topic: Logical Reasoning; Analytical Ability and Data Interpretation
questions.stem: A pump delivers 24 cubic metres per minute for 15 minutes and then 18 cubic metres per minute for 10 minutes. What is its average discharge over the full 25-minute period?
explanations: 18.0 m³/min is only the second-period rate.
20.0 m³/min understates the total volume divided by the full duration.
Correct. Total volume=24×15+18×10=540 m³; average=540/25=21.6 m³/min.
22.5 m³/min is not the weighted average over the stated durations.

questions.stem: Choose the grammatically correct completion: “No sooner had the pump started ___ the pressure indicator began to fluctuate.”
explanations: 'No sooner' is conventionally paired with 'than', not 'when'.
'Then' does not complete the standard correlative construction.
'As' is not the required conjunction in this pattern.

questions.stem: In the sentence “The engineer adopted a prudent maintenance schedule,” the word 'prudent' most nearly means:
explanations: Reckless is nearly the opposite of prudent.
Correct. Prudent means showing care, good judgement and foresight.
Unavoidable describes necessity, not judgement.
Expensive refers to cost and is not the meaning of prudent.

questions.stem: Choose the correct reported form of: The engineer said, “I am inspecting the valve now.”
options: The engineer said that I am inspecting the valve now.
The engineer said that he is inspecting the valve tomorrow.
The engineer said that he was inspecting the valve then.
The engineer said that he had inspected the valve yesterday.
explanations: The pronoun does not normally remain 'I' when reporting the engineer's statement in the third person.
The tense and time expression have not been adjusted for ordinary indirect speech.
Correct. Present progressive commonly backshifts to past progressive and 'now' changes to 'then' in this reported context.
This changes the action to past perfect and 'yesterday', which the original statement did not say.

questions.subtopic: Variance of a sum with non-zero covariance
questions.stem: Random variables X and Y have Var(X)=4, Var(Y)=9 and Cov(X,Y)=−2. What is Var(X+Y)?
explanations: 5 omits part of the variance terms.
Correct. Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y)=4+9−4=9.
13 would be the result if covariance were zero.
17 incorrectly adds the absolute covariance term instead of using its negative sign.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Probability and Statistics; source/basis: Ross, A First Course in Probability; covariance and variance of sums

questions.stem: Independent trials succeed with probability 0.25 on each trial. If X is the number of trials up to and including the first success, what is E[X]?
explanations: For a geometric distribution counted from trial 1, the mean is not 2 at p=0.25.
The expected number is greater than three for a success probability of one quarter.
Correct. E[X]=1/p=1/0.25=4 trials.
5 is not the reciprocal of the stated success probability.
